title: The next greater element
objectives: Use a monotonic stack to find the next greater element.
Explain why each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the scan is $O(n)$
Adapt the scan to days until a higher value, and choose `<` or `<=` for ties

screens.title: The next higher close
screens.prose: Seven daily closes, in pounds. For each day we want the first later day that closed higher. Start with day 3, which closed at 3.
screens.question: Tap the first value to the right of day 3 that is greater than 3.

hints.text: Look only to the right of day 3, one cell at a time.
This value comes next, but it is smaller than 3.
Day 4 closed at 1, which is lower. Day 5 closed at 5, the first value above 3.

feedback.correct: 5, on day 5, is the next value above 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move right from day 3 and stop at the first value greater than 3.

byKey.c4: 1 comes next, but it is smaller than 3. Keep moving right.
byKey.c6: 7 is greater than 3, but 5 comes earlier.
byKey.c2: 6 is greater, but it is to the left of day 3. Only later days count.
byKey.c3: That is day 3 itself. Look at the days after it.

explain.text: From day 3 you passed 1 and stopped at 5. That walk to the right is the obvious method: from each day, scan forward. Some days have to scan a long way.

screens.title: The cost of scanning ahead

state.caption: A strictly falling list: every answer is −1

screens.question: How many comparisons `xs[j] > xs[i]` does it make on these 6 values?

hints.text: How many values does the scan from day 0 look at?
From the first value there are 5 later values to compare with.
Day 0 compares with 5 values, day 1 with 4, and so on down to day 5 with none. Add them up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the later values each day compares against, then add.

byKey.square: You counted every pair $(i, j)$, all 36. The inner loop starts at $i + 1$, so it only looks forward.
byKey.linear: That is one comparison per day. In a falling list each scan runs to the end.
byKey.both-ways: You counted each pair twice. The scan only looks forward, so each pair is compared once.

explain.text: The scans cost $5 + 4 + \dots + 0 = \tfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$. For $n$ values that is $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, which is $O(n^2)$. A year of minute bars, about 100,000 closes, would need about 5 billion comparisons.

screens.title: Who is still waiting
screens.prose: Turn it round: instead of scanning ahead, let each day **wait** for its answer. We read left to right. Days 0 and 1, closing at 4 and 2, are waiting on a stack. Now day 2 closes at 6.

state.caption: Below: the stack of days still waiting

screens.question: Tap every earlier day that 6 answers.

hints.text: Which waiting values are smaller than 6?
Both waiting values are below 6.
6 is greater than both waiting values, 2 and 4. So 6 is the answer for days 0 and 1.

feedback.correct: 6 answers both waiting days, 2 first and then 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only days still waiting, to the left of day 2, can be answered.

byKey.c0: 4 is waiting too, and 6 is greater than 4. Day 0 gets its answer now.
byKey.c1: 2 is on top of the stack, and 6 is greater than 2. Day 1 gets its answer now.
byKey.c2: That is day 2 itself. It starts waiting for its own answer.
byKey.c3: Day 3 has not been read yet. 6 can only answer earlier days.
byKey.c4: Day 4 has not been read yet. 6 can only answer earlier days.
byKey.c5: Day 5 has not been read yet. 6 can only answer earlier days.
byKey.c6: Day 6 has not been read yet. 6 can only answer earlier days.

explain.text: 6 pops 2, then 4, and records 6 as the answer for both. Then day 2 starts waiting. The waiting values never rise from bottom to top, so this is called a **monotonic stack**.

canvas.caption: Days 0 and 1 answered by 6; day 2 now waits

screens.title: Run the stack
screens.prose: Carry on from day 3. The rule you used: while the new value is greater than the top, pop the top. Record the new value as the popped day's answer. Then push the new value.

state.caption: Answered days in green; the stack below

screens.question: Step the stack through days 3 to 6.

ops.label: Pop 6, then push 3
ops.why: 3 is smaller than 6, so it does not answer 6. Day 2 keeps waiting.

ops.label: Pop 3, then push 1
ops.why: 1 is smaller than 3, so it answers nobody. Push it and let it wait.

ops.label: Push 5
ops.why: 5 is greater than 1 and 3. Pushing it on top would leave them waiting under a bigger value, with their answers lost.

ops.label: Pop 1 and 3, both answered by 5, then push 5
Pop 1, 3 and 6, then push 5
ops.why: 5 is not greater than 6. Stop popping at the first top that is at least as big as 5.

ops.label: Pop 5, then push 7
ops.why: 7 is greater than 6 as well. Keep popping while the top is smaller than 7.

ops.label: Pop 5 and 6, both answered by 7, then push 7

hints.text: Compare the new value with the top of the stack. Is it greater?
The top is the most recent day still waiting.
Days 3 and 4 just push. Day 5 pops 1 and 3. Day 6 pops 5 and 6. Day 6 is left waiting, so it gets −1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pop only while the top is smaller than the new value, then push.

explain.text: Each day went onto the stack once and came off at most once. Day 5 answered two days at a single stroke, and day 6 answered two more. Day 6 was still waiting at the end, so its answer is −1.

screens.title: Falling and rising
screens.prose: Two extreme price paths: one falls every day, one rises every day.
screens.question: What does the next greater scan return for each?

options.why: You took the next value, not the next greater one. In a falling list nothing to the right is higher.
You took the largest value to the right. We want the first greater one, which here is the very next value.
In a rising list each value is popped by its neighbour straight away, so each gets an answer.

hints.text: In the falling list, is any later value higher than an earlier one?
In the rising list, the very next value is already higher.
Falling: nothing is ever popped, so all four end with −1. Rising: each value is popped by the next one, and only the last is left.

feedback.correct: Falling gives all −1; rising answers each value with its neighbour.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the stack on each path, one value at a time.

byKey.b: You recorded the next value. A falling path never has a higher close later, so every answer is −1.
byKey.c: You recorded the maximum to the right. The first greater value in a rising path is the next one.

explain.text: On the falling path the stack grows to all 4 values and nothing is popped. On the rising path each value is popped by its neighbour, so at most one day waits. Either way the work is about $2n$ steps.

canvas.caption: Falling: the stack fills. Rising: it never holds more than one.

screens.title: Ties
screens.prose:
Our convention: the next **strictly** greater value, so an equal value keeps waiting. A teammate writes the pop condition with `<=`.

```python
while stack and xs[stack[-1]] <= x:
    ans[stack.pop()] = x
```

state.caption: Two equal closes, then a higher one

screens.question: What does their `next_greater([5, 5, 6])` return?

options.why: That is what strict `<` returns. With `<=`, the second 5 pops the first, so 5 is recorded as greater than 5.
You let the second 5 pass the first. With `<=` it pops the first 5 and records itself as the answer.
6 is the last value, so nothing comes after it. It stays on the stack and gets −1.

hints.text: When the second 5 arrives, is `5 <= 5` true?
The first 5 is on top when this 5 arrives.
`<=` pops the first 5 and records 5 as its answer. Then 6 pops the second 5. 6 is left with −1.

feedback.correct: With `<=` an equal value counts as greater, which breaks the convention.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the `<=` condition on the second 5.

byKey.b: You ran the strict version. The teammate's `<=` treats the second 5 as an answer for the first.
byKey.c: You expected the tie to wait. Under `<=`, `5 <= 5` is true, so the first 5 is popped.

explain.text: `5 <= 5` is true, so the first 5 is popped with 5 as its answer, which is not greater. Use `<` and ties wait for 6. Some problems want the next value at least as high; state the convention, then pick `<` or `<=` to match.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
What you did, as code. The stack holds **indices**, so each answer can be written in place.

```python
ans = [-1] * len(xs)
stack = []  # indices still waiting
for i, x in enumerate(xs):
    while stack and xs[stack[-1]] < x:
        ans[stack.pop()] = x
    stack.append(i)
```

There is a loop inside a loop, yet the work is not $O(n^2)$.
screens.question: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once. For $n = 1{,}000$, at most how many pushes and pops are there in total?

feedback.correct: At most $2n = 2{,}000$ stack operations, so the scan is $O(n)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count pushes and pops separately.

byKey.square: You multiplied the two loops. The inner `while` can only pop what was pushed, and each index is pushed once.
byKey.half: That counts the pushes only. Each index can also be popped once.
byKey.pairs: That is the nested scan's count. The `while` never pops the same index twice.

explain.text: Each of the 1,000 indices is pushed once and popped at most once. So the `while` body runs at most 1,000 times in total. That is at most 2,000 operations: $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space for the stack.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Now write the scan without looking. Ties wait: an equal value is not greater.
screens.question: Write `next_greater(xs)`: for each position, the first later value strictly greater, or −1 if there is none.

widget.starter:
def next_greater(xs):
    ans = [-1] * len(xs)
    stack = []  # indices still waiting
    ...
    return ans

Ties wait: both 5s are answered by 6.
`for i, x in enumerate(xs):` then `while stack and xs[stack[-1]] < x: ans[stack.pop()] = x`, then `stack.append(i)`.

feedback.correct: One pass, each index pushed and popped at most once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 is `[5, 5, 6]`. You popped on a tie: use `<`, not `<=`, so equal values wait.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 timed out or failed on 200,000 falling values. A nested scan is $O(n^2)$; use the stack so each index moves at most twice.

explain.text: `ans` starts as all −1, so days still waiting at the end need no extra work. The stack holds indices, which lets `ans[stack.pop()] = x` write in place. 200,000 values take at most 400,000 stack operations.

screens.title: A famous use
screens.prose: The **largest rectangle in a histogram** is a classic interview problem. A rectangle at the full height of a bar stretches sideways until the nearest **shorter** bar on each side. So each bar needs its next smaller bar, not its next greater one.
screens.question: Which change to our scan finds the next smaller value to the right?

options.text: Pop while `xs[stack[-1]] > x`, so the stack rises from bottom to top

options.why: That pops when a bigger value arrives, which finds the next greater value.
Sorting throws away positions. "Next" is about order in the list.

options.text: Use a queue and take the oldest waiting bar first
options.why: The most recent waiting bar is the nearest one, so it must be answered first: last in, first out.

hints.text: Which arriving value should end a bar's wait now?
When the 2 at index 4 arrives, the 6 and the 5 before it have found a shorter bar.
Flip the comparison: pop while the top is taller than the new bar. The waiting bars then rise from bottom to top.

feedback.correct: Flip the comparison and the same scan finds next smaller values.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What should make a waiting bar stop waiting?

byKey.b: You kept the next greater test. A bar's rectangle ends at a shorter bar, so pop on `>`.

explain.text: With `>`, the 2 at index 4 pops the 6 and the 5. The 5 spans indices 2 and 3, so its rectangle is $5 \times 2 = 10$, the largest here. Running the scan from both sides gives each bar's width in $O(n)$.

screens.title: A breakout detector
screens.prose: A desk wants, for each day, how many days until the price next closes above today's close. The desk reads a long wait as a ceiling that held, and a short one as momentum. Days with no higher close later get 0.

state.caption: Day 0 waits until day 2, so its answer is 2

screens.question: Write `days_until_higher(prices)`: the number of days until a strictly higher close, or 0 if none comes.

widget.starter:
def days_until_higher(prices):
    ans = [0] * len(prices)
    stack = []  # indices of days still waiting
    ...
    return ans
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, including an empty list, a falling path, a rising path and a tie.

hints.text: What do you record when an index is popped: the price, or something else?
Day 1 waits for day 2: one day. Day 0 waits for day 2 as well.
Same loop as `next_greater`, but when you pop `j` at day `i`, record `i - j`.

feedback.correct: Same stack, but each answer records a distance in days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 has two equal closes then a higher one. Equal is not higher: pop on `<` only.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the table's prices. Record `i - j`, the gap in days, not the price.

explain.text: The stack holds days still waiting for a higher close. When day `i` pops day `j`, the wait was `i - j` days. This is the daily temperatures problem with prices, and it runs in $O(n)$ on years of data.

ideas: Instead of scanning ahead from every value, let values wait on a stack until something greater arrives.
The waiting values never rise from bottom to top: a monotonic stack. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the scan is $O(n)$.
Record a distance instead of a value, or flip the comparison, and the same scan solves new problems.

formula.name: Monotonic stack step
formula.note: Pushes plus pops are at most $2n$. Use `<` when ties should wait, `<=` when an equal value counts.

summary.trap: `<=` pops on a tie, so an equal value is recorded as greater. A nested scan gives the right answers but is $O(n^2)$.

quiz.prose: Run the next greater scan on `[2, 1, 3]`.
quiz.question: What does it return?

options.why: You took the next value. 1 is smaller than 2, so 2 keeps waiting until 3.
2 does get an answer: 3 comes later and is greater.
Nothing comes after the last value, so it gets −1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each value, look right for the first greater one.

explain.text: 2 waits, then 1 waits on top of it. 3 pops 1, then 2, and answers both. 3 itself is left with −1.

quiz.prose: Run the scan on the closes `[6, 4, 5, 2]`.
quiz.question: Which values are on the stack at the end, bottom to top?

options.why: 5 is greater than 4, so 5 popped 4 when it arrived.
5 is not greater than 6, so 6 was never popped.
Only values smaller than an arrival are popped. 6 and 5 are still waiting.

feedback.correct: 4 was popped by 5; the rest still wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pop only while the arriving value is greater than the top.

explain.text: 6 and 4 are pushed; 5 pops 4, stops at 6, and is pushed. Then 2 is pushed. The stack falls from bottom to top: 6, 5, 2.

quiz.prose: The scan has a `while` loop inside a `for` loop over $n$ values.
quiz.question: Why is it $O(n)$ and not $O(n^2)$?

options.text: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the `while` runs at most $n$ times in total
The `while` loop always runs at most once per value
options.why: One arrival can pop many values, as day 5 popped two. The bound is on the total, not per step.

options.text: The stack never holds more than a few values
options.why: On a falling path the stack holds all $n$ values.
Speed per operation does not change the growth rate. The count of operations does.

feedback.correct: The total work is bounded by pushes plus pops: at most $2n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how often an index can be popped over the whole run.

explain.text: A single step may pop many values, but each index is popped at most once over the whole scan. So all the `while` iterations together are at most $n$. Add $n$ pushes and the total is at most $2n$.

quiz.question: For day 0 (£100), how many days until a strictly higher close?

feedback.correct: Day 3 is the first close above £100, three days later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first later close above £100.

byKey.between: You counted the days in between. The answer is the gap in index: 3 − 0.
byKey.next: Day 1 closed lower, at £98. It is not higher than £100.

explain.text: £98 and £99 are both below £100. Day 3 closes at £101, so the wait is $3 - 0 = 3$ days.
